claims.text: The baseline Cr16Mn16Fe16Co16Ni16P20 alloy forms several primary non-eutectic crystalline phases during solidification.
The baseline alloy undergoes a complex, multistep crystallization sequence.
Approximately 2 at.% Nb is proposed as an addition to the baseline alloy.
Nb will act as a nucleation inhibitor during rapid and slower cooling.
Nb has an atomic-size and bonding mismatch relative to the constituents of the baseline alloy.
Nb atoms will segregate at potential nucleation sites.
Nb segregation will disrupt local atomic ordering and increase chemical heterogeneity.
The Nb addition will raise the nucleation-energy barrier by interfering with the local structural order required to form primary crystalline phases.
The Nb-induced structural disruption will delay crystallite formation during cooling.
The Nb-induced structural disruption will delay crystallization during subsequent reheating.
Adding Nb will broaden the processing window for glass formation and improve thermal stability.
The Nb-modified alloy will retain a higher amorphous-phase fraction than the undoped alloy under comparable processing conditions.
On reheating, the Nb-modified alloy will have a higher crystallization-onset temperature than the undoped alloy.
On reheating, the Nb-modified alloy will exhibit a less pronounced crystallization exotherm, indicating improved thermal stability.
The baseline alloy exhibits extensive primary crystallization under both rapid and slower cooling.
The proposed intervention is intended to be effective at cooling rates of approximately 10^3 to 10^5 K/s.
The relevant reheating interval extends from just below the glass-transition temperature to the crystallization-onset temperature.
Outside the stated cooling-rate and reheating boundaries, the benefits of Nb may not occur.
A higher glass-transition temperature is proposed as evidence of increased amorphous-phase retention.

contradictions.description: The test conditions define rapid cooling as at least 10^5 K/s and slower cooling as below 10^3 K/s, whereas the claimed effective boundary is 10^3–10^5 K/s. Thus, most of the explicitly proposed rapid and slower test regimes lie outside the stated effective interval.
